final.final_answer:
From the Utility Types reference (previous steps) and the current Handbook > Keyof Type Operator page, here is the requested comparison and the keyof relationship, using only what is visible in the TypeScript docs.

1) Pick<Type, Keys>
- Generic signature (from Utility Types page section heading):
  - Pick<Type, Keys>
- What it keeps/removes:
  - Constructs a type by **keeping only** the properties from Type whose keys are in Keys.
  - Keys is a union of property names; properties not listed in Keys are removed.
- First displayed example and result (from the Pick section’s first example block):
  - Code:
    - `interface Todo {`
    - `  title: string;`
    - `  description: string;`
    - `  completed: boolean;`
    - `}`
    - `type TodoPreview = Pick<Todo, "title" | "completed">;`
  - Result shown in the inline evaluation in that same code block:
    - `type TodoPreview = { title: string; completed: boolean; }`
  - Interpretation:
    - Only the `title` and `completed` keys from `Todo` are kept; `description` is removed.

2) Omit<Type, Keys>
- Generic signature (from Utility Types page section heading):
  - Omit<Type, Keys>
- What it keeps/removes:
  - Constructs a type by **removing** the properties from Type whose keys are in Keys, and **keeping all the remaining** properties.
- First displayed example and result (top of the Omit section’s code block):
  - Code:
    - `interface Todo {`
    - `  title: string;`
    - `  description: string;`
    - `  completed: boolean;`
    - `  createdAt: number;`
    - `}`
    - `type TodoPreview = Omit<Todo, "description">;`
    - `const todo: TodoPreview = {`
    - `  title: "Clean room",`
    - `  completed: false,`
    - `  createdAt: 1615544252770,`
    - `};`
    - `todo;`
  - Result shown next to the first alias in that block:
    - `type TodoPreview = { title: string; completed: boolean; createdAt: number; }`
  - Interpretation:
    - `description` is removed from `Todo`; `title`, `completed`, and `createdAt` are kept.

3) Exclude<UnionType, ExcludedMembers>
- Generic signature (from Utility Types page section heading):
  - Exclude<UnionType, ExcludedMembers>
- What it keeps/removes:
  - From a union type UnionType, it **removes** any union members that are assignable to ExcludedMembers.
  - The remaining members of the original union are kept.
- First displayed example and result (top of the Exclude section):
  - Code and inline result:
    - `type T0 = Exclude<"a" | "b" | "c", "a">;`
    - `type T0 = "b" | "c"`
  - Interpretation:
    - Starting from `"a" | "b" | "c"`, the member `"a"` is excluded, leaving `"b" | "c"`.

4) Extract<Type, Union>
- Generic signature (from Utility Types page section heading):
  - Extract<Type, Union>
- What it keeps/removes:
  - From a union Type, it **keeps only** those members that are assignable to Union, removing the rest.
- First displayed example and result (top of the Extract section):
  - Code and inline result:
    - `type T0 = Extract<"a" | "b" | "c", "a" | "f">;`
    - `type T0 = "a"`
  - Interpretation:
    - The overlap between `"a" | "b" | "c"` and `"a" | "f"` is just `"a"`, so the result keeps only `"a"`.

5) keyof type operator (Handbook > Keyof Type Operator page)

What keyof produces (from the visible examples)
- The page text states (paraphrasing from the visible heading section):
  - “The `keyof` operator takes an object type and **produces a string or numeric literal union of its keys**.”
- First example code block on the page:
  - `type Point = { x: number; y: number };`
  - `type P = keyof Point;`
  - Inline evaluated result shown directly in the same block:
    - `type P = keyof Point`
    - And the preceding explanation clarifies that this is the same as:
      - `type P = "x" | "y"`
  - Interpretation:
    - For the object type `Point` with properties `x` and `y`, `keyof Point` yields the union of those property names: `"x" | "y"`.

- Second example code block (index signatures):
  - `type Arrayish = { [n: number]: unknown };`
  - `type A = keyof Arrayish;`
  - Inline result shown:
    - `type A = number`
  - Then, immediately following in the same block:
    - `type Mapish = { [k: string]: boolean };`
    - `type M = keyof Mapish;`
    - Inline result shown:
      - `type M = string | number`
  - Interpretation:
    - If a type has a **number index signature**, `keyof` yields `number`.
    - If it has a **string index signature**, `keyof` yields `string | number` (the text notes this is because JavaScript object keys are always coerced to strings, so numeric keys behave like strings and both appear in the union).

6) How keyof relates to Pick and Omit (per the displayed examples)

Link from keyof examples to Pick
- From the keyof page’s first example:
  - `type Point = { x: number; y: number };`
  - `type P = keyof Point;` → conceptually `type P = "x" | "y"`.
- From the Pick utility type example:
  - `interface Todo { title: string; description: string; completed: boolean; }`
  - `type TodoPreview = Pick<Todo, "title" | "completed">;`
- The keyof example shows that `keyof SomeObjectType` gives a **union of valid property names** for that type. The Pick example shows Keys being written as a literal union of property names.
- Putting the two visible examples together:
  - `keyof Todo` would be a union of all the property names of `Todo`.
  - The Keys argument in `Pick<Todo, "title" | "completed">` is exactly the kind of union that `keyof Todo` defines: a union of keys from `Todo`.
  - Thus, according to the examples, `keyof` defines the **space of legal Keys** you can use with Pick. Pick then uses that subset of keys to keep only those properties.

Link from keyof examples to Omit
- The Omit example’s first alias:
  - `type TodoPreview = Omit<Todo, "description">;`
  - Result: `type TodoPreview = { title: string; completed: boolean; createdAt: number; }` (description removed).
- From the keyof page, we see:
  - `keyof` enumerates all keys of a type as a union (e.g., `"x" | "y"` for `Point`).
  - For types with index signatures, it gives unions like `number` or `string | number`.
- Combining these visible facts:
  - `keyof Todo` would give the union of all keys on `Todo`.
  - Omit’s behavior in the example matches what you would get by:
    - Starting from `keyof Todo` (all keys),
    - Conceptually removing the listed Keys (`"description"`),
    - Then keeping the remaining keys’ properties.
  - While the exact `Omit` definition isn’t shown on the keyof page, the combination of:
    - the keyof examples (showing how to get the full key union), and
    - the Omit example (showing that it removes specified keys while keeping the rest)
    demonstrates that Omit is effectively operating over the union that `keyof` would produce.

Summarized relationship, grounded in the docs’ examples
- `keyof` (Handbook page examples):
  - Takes an object type (like `Point` or an index-signature type) and yields a **union of its property keys** (e.g., `"x" | "y"`, `number`, or `string | number`).
- `Pick` (Utility Types examples):
  - Uses a **subset** of that key union (e.g., `"title" | "completed"`) to **keep only** those properties on a type.
  - The keyof examples explain exactly what kinds of unions (of keys) are valid and how they’re derived from a type.
- `Omit` (Utility Types examples):
  - Uses a set of keys (e.g., `"description"`) to **remove** those properties and keep the rest.
  - Conceptually, given the keyof examples, it acts over the `keyof`-derived union of keys by subtracting the specified ones, leaving the remaining keys that its resulting type keeps.

Together, the visible docs show that:
- `keyof` defines the **universe of property names** available on a type as a union.
- `Pick` chooses some of those keys to keep.
- `Omit` chooses some of those keys to drop and keeps everything else.
- The handbook examples (especially `type P = keyof Point;`) and utility type examples (like `Pick<Todo, "title" | "completed">` and `Omit<Todo, "description">`) illustrate how these operators and utilities are conceptually connected via unions of property keys.

Exclude<UnionType, ExcludedMembers> removes union members assignable to ExcludedMembers; first example `T0 = Exclude<"a" | "b" | "c", "a">` → `"b" | "c"`. Extract<Type, Union> keeps only overlapping union members; first example `T0 = Extract<"a" | "b" | "c", "a" | "f">` → `"a"`. Keyof Type Operator page verified examples: `type Point = { x: number; y: number }; type P = keyof Point;` with text explaining this is `"x" | "y"`; second block `type Arrayish = { [n: number]: unknown }; type A = keyof Arrayish;` → `number`; `type Mapish = { [k: string]: boolean }; type M = keyof Mapish;` → `string | number`. Relationship: keyof yields union of keys; Pick takes subset of such unions to keep properties; Omit removes some keys from that key space and keeps the rest.
